Pathology 03.question: ১) Which one is the most important cause of NGU?
Pathology 03.exp:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU), especially in sexually active young adults.

NGU presents with dysuria and urethral discharge, but without evidence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Why the other options are less likely:

  • Trichomonas vaginalis: Can cause urethritis but is a less common cause of NGU.

  • Herpes simplex virus: May cause urethritis, but is uncommon.

  • Ureaplasma: Can be associated with NGU, but C. trachomatis is the classic and most important cause.

High-yield STI recall:
NGU → Chlamydia trachomatis is the classic exam association.
Other causes include Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis.

Exam pearl:
Most important/common cause of NGU = Chlamydia trachomatis.

Pathology 03.question: ২) Which is one is not a features of hypovolemic shock?
Pathology 03.exp:
Hypovolemic shock causes reduced circulating volume and decreased renal perfusion. The body activates sympathetic nervous system, RAAS, and ADH, resulting in water and sodium retention and therefore oliguria, not polyuria.

Typical features include:

  • Hypotension

  • Tachycardia

  • Cold, clammy periphery

  • Oliguria

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Hypotension: Due to reduced circulating volume and cardiac output.

  • Tachycardia: Compensatory sympathetic response.

  • Cold periphery: Due to peripheral vasoconstriction.

High-yield Shock recall:
Hypovolemic shock → hypotension + tachycardia + cold periphery + oliguria.

Exam pearl:
Shock → renal hypoperfusion → oliguria, not polyuria.

Pathology 03.question: ৩) Bacterial spores are destroyed by following process excludes...?
Pathology 03.exp:
Bacterial spores are highly resistant structures and are not reliably destroyed by pasteurization. Pasteurization is designed primarily to reduce vegetative pathogenic microorganisms in foods and beverages, not to achieve sterilization.

The following methods can destroy spores when appropriately performed:

  • Autoclaving: Moist heat under pressure; reliably destroys spores.

  • Hot air oven: Dry heat sterilization; destroys spores with adequate temperature and exposure.

  • Gamma radiation: Ionizing radiation capable of sterilizing many medical products, including destruction of spores.

Why pasteurization is incorrect:
Pasteurization uses relatively low temperatures and therefore does not reliably eliminate bacterial spores.

High-yield Sterilization recall:
Pasteurization ≠ sterilization. It reduces pathogens but generally does not destroy spores.

Exam pearl:
Bacterial spores survive pasteurization; autoclave, dry heat, and gamma radiation can destroy them.

Pathology 03.question: ৪) In which of the following disease, immunity may be acquired by subclinical infection?
Pathology 03.exp:
In diphtheria, immunity can be acquired following a subclinical or inapparent infection. The infection may stimulate production of antitoxin antibodies, even when the person has minimal or no obvious clinical illness.

The other diseases are more typically associated with clinically apparent infection, although rubella can also be asymptomatic/subclinical in a substantial proportion of cases.

Why the other options are less appropriate:

  • Chickenpox: Usually produces a characteristic clinical illness with vesicular rash.

  • Rubella: Often asymptomatic, so this option can be confusing; however, the classic exam association for immunity following subclinical infection is diphtheria.

  • Measles: Usually causes a prominent symptomatic illness.

High-yield Immunization recall:
Diphtheria infection → antitoxin immunity may develop even after subclinical infection.

Exam pearl:
Subclinical diphtheria infection can produce natural antitoxin immunity.

Pathology 03.question: ৫) Which one is not correct regarding active immunity?
Pathology 03.exp:
Active immunity develops when the immune system is stimulated to produce its own antibodies and memory cells, either through natural infection or vaccination.

Its important features include:

  • Long-lasting protection due to immunological memory.

  • Generally more effective and durable protection.

  • Often cost-effective because protection can persist for a long period.

  • Severe reactions are not generally common; most vaccine reactions are mild and transient.

Therefore, “severe reaction is common” is the incorrect statement.

High-yield Immunology recall:
Active immunity → slow onset + long-lasting + immunological memory.
Passive immunity → immediate protection + short-lived + no immune memory.

Exam pearl:
Active immunity is long-lasting; severe reactions are not a defining/common feature.

Pathology 03.question: ৬) Features of gastrointestinal mucosal toxicity due to radiation exposure excludes..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Gastrointestinal mucosal toxicity from significant radiation exposure occurs because rapidly dividing intestinal epithelial cells are highly radiosensitive. Typical manifestations include:

  • Profound diarrhoea due to severe mucosal injury

  • Vomiting due to GI tract and systemic radiation injury

  • Sepsis due to disruption of the intestinal mucosal barrier and bacterial translocation

GIT bleeding is not considered a characteristic primary feature of acute GI radiation toxicity, making it the best answer for the exception.

High-yield Radiation recall:
GI radiation syndrome → nausea/vomiting + severe diarrhoea + dehydration + mucosal barrier breakdown → sepsis.

Exam pearl:
Acute GI radiation injury classically causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea with risk of sepsis.

Pathology 03.question: ৭) Which Elements contribute to herd immunity?
Pathology 03.option1: Occurrence of clinical and subclinical infection
Pathology 03.exp:
Herd immunity refers to the reduction in transmission of an infectious disease when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune.

All three factors contribute:

  • Clinical and subclinical infection: Natural infection can produce immunity in individuals.

  • Immunization of the herd: Vaccination increases the proportion of immune individuals and is the major controllable factor.

  • Herd structure: Population density, age distribution, mixing patterns, and immunity distribution influence transmission.

Therefore, all of the above contribute to herd immunity.

High-yield Public Health recall:
Herd immunity depends on the proportion immune, the infectiousness of the pathogen, and population mixing/structure.

Exam pearl:
Herd immunity = natural immunity + vaccine-induced immunity + population structure/mixing.

Pathology 03.question: ৮) Which type of vaccine used in HBV?
Pathology 03.exp:
The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant subunit vaccine. It contains hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) produced using recombinant DNA technology, commonly in yeast cells.

It is not a live virus vaccine and cannot cause HBV infection.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Live attenuated: HBV vaccine does not contain live attenuated HBV.

  • Killed: It is not an inactivated whole-virus vaccine.

  • Toxoid: Toxoid vaccines are made from inactivated bacterial toxins, e.g., diphtheria and tetanus.

High-yield Vaccine recall:
HBV vaccine = recombinant HBsAg subunit vaccine.

Exam pearl:
Hepatitis B vaccine → Recombinant DNA technology → HBsAg.

Pathology 03.question: ৯) Unprotected miners of radioactive elements have a 10 fold increased risk of..... cancer?
Pathology 03.exp:
Unprotected miners of radioactive elements, especially uranium miners, have a markedly increased risk of lung cancer due to exposure to radon and its radioactive decay products. Radon emits alpha particles, which can cause DNA damage in the respiratory epithelium.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Stomach: Not the characteristic occupational malignancy in uranium miners.

  • Bladder: More classically associated with certain chemical occupational exposures.

  • Genital: Not the characteristic cancer associated with radioactive-element mining.

High-yield Radiation recall:
Uranium mining → radon exposure → alpha radiation → lung cancer.

Exam pearl:
Unprotected uranium/radon miners → increased risk of lung cancer.

Pathology 03.question: ১০) Adverse reaction following BCG vaccine administration excludes..?
Pathology 03.exp:
The BCG vaccine is a live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis vaccine. Its characteristic adverse reactions are mainly local and mycobacterial complications, including:

  • Suppurative lymphadenitis → usually regional lymph node involvement.

  • Osteitis/osteomyelitis → rare complication.

  • Disseminated BCG infection → very rare, especially in patients with significant immunodeficiency.

Anaphylaxis is not a characteristic adverse reaction of BCG and is extremely rare.

High-yield Vaccine adverse effects recall:
BCG → local ulcer + regional lymphadenitis; rare osteitis and disseminated infection.

Exam pearl:
BCG adverse effects are predominantly mycobacterial; anaphylaxis is not a characteristic complication.

Pathology 03.question: ১১) Detection of blood in urine by..?
Pathology 03.exp:
The orthotolidine test is a traditional chemical test for detecting blood/hemoglobin in urine. It is based on the peroxidase-like activity of hemoglobin, producing a color change in the presence of an oxidizing agent.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Benedict's test: Detects reducing sugars in urine, especially glucose.

  • Rothera's test: Detects ketone bodies in urine.

  • Fouchet's test: Detects bilirubin in urine.

High-yield Urine test recall:

Test Detects
Orthotolidine Blood/hemoglobin
Benedict's Reducing sugar
Rothera's Ketone bodies
Fouchet's Bilirubin

Exam pearl:
Urinary blood → Orthotolidine test.

Pathology 03.question: ১২) Which one is correct regarding benedict test interpretation?
Pathology 03.exp:
Benedict’s test detects reducing sugars in urine. The original blue color changes according to the amount of reducing sugar present:

  • Blue → Nil/negative

  • Green → +

  • Yellow → ++

  • Orange → +++

  • Brick red → ++++

Therefore, “blue: nil” is the correct statement.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Yellow: + → Incorrect; classically yellow = ++.

  • Green: ++ → Incorrect; green = +.

  • Brick red: +++ → Incorrect; brick red = ++++.

High-yield Urine test recall:
Benedict’s test:
Blue → Green → Yellow → Orange → Brick red
= increasing amount of reducing sugar.

Exam pearl:
Benedict’s blue color = negative (no reducing sugar).

Pathology 03.question: ১৩) Spider web clot of CSF found in which type of meningitis?
Pathology 03.exp:
A spider-web (cobweb) clot forms when CSF from a patient with tuberculous meningitis is allowed to stand, classically due to the formation of a delicate fibrin web.

Typical CSF findings in TB meningitis:

  • Lymphocytic pleocytosis

  • High protein

  • Low glucose

  • Spider-web/cobweb clot on standing

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Bacterial meningitis: Usually neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose; spider-web clot is not characteristic.

  • Viral meningitis: Usually lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.

  • Fungal meningitis: May resemble TB meningitis but the classic spider-web clot is associated with TB.

High-yield Meningitis recall:
TB meningitis → lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose + cobweb clot.

Exam pearl:
Spider-web clot in CSF = Tuberculous meningitis.

Pathology 03.question: ১৪) False positive occult blood test found in which of the following condition?
Pathology 03.exp:
Traditional fecal occult blood tests (FOBT), particularly guaiac-based tests, can give false-positive results due to certain dietary substances with peroxidase activity, classically red meat and some vegetables.

Iron-containing food itself does not generally cause a false-positive guaiac test; however, this is a common exam-oriented association in older clinical MCQs.

Among the given options, iron-containing diet is the intended answer.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Carcinoma colon: Can cause true-positive occult GI bleeding.

  • Carcinoma stomach: Can cause true-positive occult GI bleeding.

  • Ulcerative colitis: Can cause true-positive occult blood due to mucosal bleeding.

High-yield GI test recall:
Guaiac FOBT false positives → dietary peroxidases (e.g., red meat, some vegetables).

Exam pearl:
For this classical MCQ, choose iron-containing diet, but remember that modern FIT (fecal immunochemical test) is not affected by dietary peroxidase activity.

Pathology 03.question: ১৫) Ketonuria may occur in which of the following condition??
Pathology 03.exp:
Ketonuria occurs when the body shifts from glucose utilization to fat metabolism, producing excess ketone bodies.

In long-standing starvation, glycogen stores become depleted, so the body uses fatty acids for energy, leading to increased ketone production and ketonuria.

Why the other options are less appropriate:

  • Uraemia: Not a typical cause of ketonuria.

  • Alcoholism: Can cause alcoholic ketoacidosis, which may produce ketonuria, but the classic answer here is starvation.

  • Obesity: Obesity alone does not typically cause ketonuria.

High-yield Urine/Metabolism recall:
Common causes of ketonuria:

  • Starvation

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis

  • Prolonged vomiting

  • Alcoholic ketoacidosis

Exam pearl:
Long-standing starvation → fat metabolism → ketone bodies → ketonuria.

Pathology 03.question: ১৬) Granular yellowish colour sputum found in..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Granular yellowish sputum containing characteristic “sulfur granules” is classically seen in pulmonary actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces species.

These yellow sulfur granules are actually colonies of the organism, not elemental sulfur.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Anthracosis: Causes black pigmentation of tissues/sputum due to carbon deposition.

  • Pseudomonas: May produce greenish/blue-green sputum due to pigments such as pyocyanin.

  • Pneumonia: Sputum may be purulent, but yellow granular/sulfur granules specifically suggest actinomycosis.

High-yield Respiratory recall:
Actinomycosis → sulfur granules → yellow granular sputum.

Exam pearl:
Yellow “sulfur granules” in sputum = pulmonary actinomycosis.

Pathology 03.question: ১৭) Which ranks 1st among the cause of death in ICU?
Pathology 03.exp:
Sepsis and septic shock are major causes of death among critically ill patients in the ICU, particularly because they can rapidly progress to multiorgan dysfunction and multiple organ failure.

  • MI: Important cause of mortality but not the classic leading ICU cause in this context.

  • Anaphylactic shock: Potentially fatal but relatively uncommon.

  • Stroke: Major cause of mortality overall but not the classic answer for ICU mortality in this question.

High-yield Critical care recall:
Septic shock → systemic inflammation + vasodilation + tissue hypoperfusion → MODS → high mortality.

Exam pearl:
Classic exam answer: Septic shock is the leading cause of death in the ICU.

Pathology 03.question: ১৮) Polyuria occurs when urine volume is more than....... L?
Pathology 03.exp:
Polyuria is defined as an abnormally increased urine output of more than 3 L/day in an adult.

  • Normal urine output: approximately 1–2 L/day

  • Polyuria: >3 L/day

  • Oliguria: <400 mL/day

  • Anuria: <100 mL/day

High-yield Renal recall:
Polyuria >3 L/day in adults.

Exam pearl:
Urine output >3 L/day = Polyuria.

Pathology 03.question: ১৯) VDRL test is positive in...% case of secondary syphilis?
Pathology 03.exp:
The VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test is a non-treponemal test used for screening and monitoring syphilis treatment.

In secondary syphilis, the VDRL test has very high sensitivity, classically quoted as approximately 98%.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • 90% / 95%: Lower than the classical sensitivity quoted for secondary syphilis.

  • 100%: Sensitivity is very high but not absolutely 100%.

High-yield Syphilis recall:
VDRL/RPR sensitivity:

  • Primary syphilis → lower sensitivity

  • Secondary syphilis → ~98%

  • Latent/tertiary → sensitivity decreases

Exam pearl:
Secondary syphilis → VDRL positive in approximately 98% of cases.

Pathology 03.question: ২০) Which one is the most dangerous among 4 types of malaria?
Pathology 03.exp:
P. falciparum causes the most severe and potentially fatal form of malaria. It can produce cerebral malaria, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, and multiorgan failure.

Its severity is largely due to sequestration of parasitized RBCs in small blood vessels, causing microvascular obstruction and tissue hypoxia.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • P. vivax: Usually less severe, but severe vivax malaria can occasionally occur.

  • P. malariae: Generally causes a milder, chronic infection.

  • P. ovale: Usually causes relatively mild disease and can cause relapse due to hypnozoites.

High-yield Malaria recall:
P. falciparum → severe malaria + cerebral malaria + highest mortality.

Exam pearl:
Most dangerous malaria = Plasmodium falciparum.

Pathology 03.question: ২১) Currently which is the most frequent etiology for septic shock?
Pathology 03.exp:
Currently, Gram-positive bacteria are generally the most frequent bacterial cause of sepsis and septic shock, particularly due to organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species.

Historically, Gram-negative bacteria were emphasized because of endotoxin (LPS), but epidemiology has shifted with increasing healthcare-associated infections, invasive procedures, and antimicrobial resistance.

Why the other options are less likely:

  • Gram-negative bacteria: Still major causes of septic shock, especially in abdominal and urinary infections, but overall frequency has generally been surpassed by Gram-positive organisms.

  • Fungi: Important in immunocompromised and critically ill patients but less frequent overall.

  • Parasites: Much less common as a cause of septic shock.

High-yield Sepsis recall:
Modern epidemiology → Gram-positive organisms are commonest bacterial causes of sepsis/septic shock.

Exam pearl:
Current commonest etiology of septic shock = Gram-positive bacteria.

Pathology 03.question: ২২) Complication of falciparum malaria excludes..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Falciparum malaria can cause severe malaria with multiple life-threatening complications. Hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia, is a recognized complication, particularly in severe malaria and during quinine therapy.

Important complications include:

  • Hyperpyrexia

  • Severe hemolytic anemia

  • Acute renal failure (ARF)

  • Cerebral malaria

  • Metabolic acidosis

  • Hypoglycemia

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Hyperpyrexia: Can occur in severe falciparum malaria.

  • Severe anemia: Due to hemolysis and destruction of parasitized and non-parasitized RBCs.

  • ARF: A recognized complication of severe falciparum malaria.

High-yield Malaria recall:
Severe falciparum malaria → cerebral malaria + severe anemia + hypoglycemia + ARF + acidosis + pulmonary edema/ARDS.

Exam pearl:
Falciparum malaria → think HYPOglycemia, not hyperglycemia.

Pathology 03.question: ২৩) Hay's surface tension test is done to detect..... in stool?
Pathology 03.exp:
Hay’s surface tension test is used to detect bile salts in stool.

Bile salts reduce the surface tension of water. When sulfur powder is sprinkled over stool suspension, it sinks if bile salts are present because the reduced surface tension allows the sulfur to penetrate the surface.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Reducing substances: Detected by tests such as Benedict’s test.

  • Bilirubin: Detected by specific chemical tests.

  • Blood: Detected by occult blood tests such as guaiac-based tests.

High-yield Stool test recall:
Hay’s test → Bile salts in stool.

Exam pearl:
Hay’s surface tension test = detection of bile salts.

Pathology 03.question: ২৪) Which one is diagnostic criteria of severe malaria according to national guideline?
Pathology 03.exp:
According to standard severe malaria criteria, repeated generalized convulsions (classically more than 2 episodes in 24 hours) are a criterion of severe malaria.

  • Urine output <400 mL/24 h indicates oliguria and can be a feature of severe malaria when associated with acute kidney injury, but the wording here is not the classic defining criterion.

  • Hematocrit >15% is not a criterion for severe malaria. Severe malaria is associated with severe anemia, e.g. markedly reduced hemoglobin/hematocrit.

Therefore, all are not true.

High-yield Malaria recall:
Severe malaria features include repeated convulsions, impaired consciousness/coma, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema/ARDS, shock, hemoglobinuria, and acute kidney injury/oliguria.

Exam pearl:
Repeated generalized convulsions (>2/24 h) = severe malaria criterion.

Pathology 03.question: ২৫) Which of the following is not a cause of reactionary haemorrhage?
Pathology 03.exp:
Reactionary hemorrhage occurs usually within 24 hours after surgery or trauma. Common causes include:

  • Slippage of ligature

  • Dislodgement of clot

  • Normalization/rise of blood pressure

Infection causes secondary hemorrhage, typically several days later, due to infection-related tissue necrosis and erosion of the vessel wall.

High-yield Hemorrhage recall:
Reactionary → ligature slip + clot dislodgement + BP normalization
Secondary → infection → vessel erosion

Exam pearl:
Infection is a cause of secondary, not reactionary, hemorrhage.

Pathology 03.question: ২৬) Visceral leishmaniasis is the result of which parasitic manifestation?
Pathology 03.exp:
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is classically caused by the Leishmania donovani complex, particularly L. donovani in the Indian subcontinent.

It primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, especially the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, causing fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • L. tropica: Mainly causes cutaneous leishmaniasis.

  • L. mexicana: Causes cutaneous leishmaniasis.

  • L. braziliensis: Classically associated with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis.

High-yield Parasitology recall:
L. donovani → visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)
L. tropica → cutaneous leishmaniasis
L. braziliensis → mucocutaneous leishmaniasis

Exam pearl:
Kala-azar = Leishmania donovani.

Pathology 03.question: ২৭) Which one is not a cardinal features of kala-azar?
Pathology 03.exp:
The cardinal features suggesting visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) include:

  • Prolonged fever

  • Weight loss

  • Anemia/pancytopenia

  • Splenomegaly

  • History of residing in or travelling to an endemic area

However, “fever >5 days” is not a specific cardinal criterion for kala-azar. Kala-azar typically causes prolonged fever for weeks, often with splenomegaly.

Why the other options are appropriate:

  • Weight loss: Common feature.

  • Anemia: Common due to marrow involvement, hypersplenism, and chronic disease.

  • Residing/travelling in endemic area: Important epidemiological clue.

High-yield Kala-azar recall:
Prolonged fever + massive splenomegaly + weight loss + pancytopenia + endemic exposure → visceral leishmaniasis.

Exam pearl:
Kala-azar classically presents with prolonged fever, splenomegaly, weight loss, and anemia.

Pathology 03.question: ২৮) Massive proteinuria occurs when more than...... gm of albumin passes through urine in 24 hours?
Pathology 03.exp:
Massive (nephrotic-range) proteinuria is defined as urinary protein loss of >3.5 g/24 hours in an adult.

This level of proteinuria is a major feature of nephrotic syndrome, along with:

  • Hypoalbuminemia

  • Generalized edema

  • Hyperlipidemia

  • Lipiduria

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • 2.5 g: Below the nephrotic range.

  • 4.5 g / 5.5 g: These are above the threshold but are not the defining cutoff.

High-yield Renal recall:
Nephrotic-range proteinuria = >3.5 g/day in adults.

Exam pearl:
Proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h = nephrotic-range (massive) proteinuria

Pathology 03.question: ২৯) Which is the most common form of shock?
Pathology 03.exp:
Hypovolemic shock is classically considered the most common type of shock, caused by a significant reduction in circulating blood volume.

Common causes include:

  • Hemorrhage

  • Severe vomiting/diarrhea

  • Dehydration

  • Extensive burns

High-yield Shock recall:

  • Hypovolemic → loss of circulating volume

  • Cardiogenic → pump failure

  • Distributive → abnormal vasodilation (e.g., septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic)

  • Obstructive → mechanical obstruction to circulation

Exam pearl:
Most common type of shock = Hypovolemic shock.

Pathology 03.question: ৩০) Dose of oral miltefosine in adult is...?
Pathology 03.exp:
For visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), oral miltefosine is given in adults at approximately 2.5 mg/kg/day, usually for 28 days.

High-yield Leishmaniasis recall:
Miltefosine → oral antileishmanial drug → ~2.5 mg/kg/day in adults.

Exam pearl:
Adult oral miltefosine dose = 2.5 mg/kg body weight/day.

Pathology 03.question: ৩১) ‘Filariform larva' is the infective form of which worm?
Pathology 03.exp:
Filariform larva (L3 larva) is the infective stage of hookworms, mainly Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.

The filariform larva is non-feeding and usually infects humans by penetrating the skin, commonly through bare feet.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis): Infective stage is the embryonated egg.

  • Roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides): Infective stage is the embryonated egg containing L2 larva.

  • Tapeworm: Infective forms vary depending on the species, but not filariform larva.

High-yield Parasitology recall:
Hookworm → infective stage = Filariform (L3) larva → skin penetration.

Exam pearl:
Filariform larva = infective stage of Hookworm.

Pathology 03.question: ৩২) In CBC report, what type of abnormality is found in ascariasis?
Pathology 03.exp:
In ascariasis, the CBC may show eosinophilia, particularly during the larval migration phase through the lungs. Helminthic infections commonly stimulate a Th2 immune response, leading to increased eosinophils.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Neutropenia: Not characteristic of ascariasis.

  • Lymphocytosis: Not the typical CBC finding.

  • No abnormality: Eosinophilia may be present, especially during tissue migration.

High-yield Parasitology recall:
Helminthic infection → eosinophilia, especially during tissue-invasive/migratory stages.

Exam pearl:
Ascariasis → eosinophilia.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৩) Haemorrhage that occurs within 24 hours are called......Haemorrhage?
Pathology 03.exp:
Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours after an injury or operation, commonly due to:

  • Slippage of a ligature

  • Dislodgement of a clot

  • Rise/normalization of blood pressure after initial hypotension

Classification by timing:

  • Primary hemorrhage: Immediate bleeding at the time of injury/operation.

  • Reactionary hemorrhage: Within 24 hours.

  • Secondary hemorrhage: Usually 5–14 days later, commonly due to infection and vessel erosion.

Exam pearl:
Within 24 hours → Reactionary hemorrhage.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৪) Presenting problem in sexually transmitted infection in male excludes..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Common presenting problems of STIs in males include:

  • Urethral discharge → commonly due to gonorrhea or chlamydia.

  • Genital ulcer → e.g., syphilis, chancroid, genital herpes.

  • Proctitis → can occur with rectal STI infections, especially in receptive anal intercourse.

Lower abdominal pain is more characteristic of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in females, rather than a typical presenting syndrome of STI in males.

High-yield STI recall:
Male STI syndromes → urethral discharge + genital ulcer + scrotal swelling + inguinal bubo + proctitis.

Exam pearl:
Male STI presenting problems do not classically include lower abdominal pain.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৫) Which of the following endocrine disorders causes shock ...... ?
Pathology 03.exp:
Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) can cause adrenal crisis, which may lead to severe hypotension and shock.

Loss of cortisol and aldosterone causes:

  • Hypotension

  • Hypovolemia due to sodium and water loss

  • Hyperkalemia

  • Hypoglycemia

  • Circulatory collapse in severe cases

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Acromegaly: Excess GH in adults; not a typical cause of shock.

  • Gigantism: Excess GH before epiphyseal closure; not a typical cause of shock.

  • Cushing's syndrome: Excess cortisol generally causes hypertension, not adrenal shock.

High-yield Endocrine recall:
Addisonian crisis → hypotension + electrolyte disturbance + hypoglycemia → shock.

Exam pearl:
Endocrine disorder classically causing shock = Addison's disease.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৬) All of the followings are the cause of cardiogenic shock except..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Cardiogenic shock occurs due to severe cardiac pump failure. Important causes include:

  • Myocardial infarction → most common cause.

  • Cardiac dysrhythmias → severe tachyarrhythmia/bradyarrhythmia can markedly reduce cardiac output.

  • Valvular heart disease → acute severe valvular dysfunction can cause pump failure.

Hypertension (HTN) is not a typical direct cause of cardiogenic shock. In fact, severe cardiogenic shock is usually associated with hypotension.

High-yield Shock recall:
Cardiogenic shock → MI + severe arrhythmia + severe valvular disease.

Exam pearl:
HTN is not a typical cause of cardiogenic shock.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৭) Which one is the most common cause of genital ulcer?
Pathology 03.exp:
Genital herpes (HSV infection) is the most common cause of genital ulcer disease in many settings.

Typical features:

  • Multiple painful vesicles that rupture to form ulcers

  • Burning/tingling may precede the lesions

  • Recurrent episodes are common

Why the other options are less likely:

  • Primary syphilis: Usually causes a single, painless, clean-based chancre.

  • Chancroid: Causes painful ulcers with ragged edges, but is less common in many regions.

  • Granuloma inguinale: Causes painless, progressive beefy-red ulcers and is relatively uncommon.

High-yield STI recall:
Genital ulcer disease → HSV is the commonest cause.

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of genital ulcer = Genital herpes (HSV).

Pathology 03.question: ৩৮) Which one is the causative factor for genital warts?
Pathology 03.exp:
Genital warts (condyloma acuminata) are caused by Human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly HPV types 6 and 11.

  • HPV 6, 11 → genital warts

  • HPV 16, 18 → strongly associated with cervical and other anogenital cancers

Exam pearl:
Genital wart → HPV, especially types 6 & 11.

Pathology 03.question: ৩৯) What type of shock occurs due to anaesthetics?
Pathology 03.exp:
Anaesthetic drugs, especially those causing sympathetic blockade, can produce marked vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, resulting in neurogenic/distributive shock.

Typical features include:

  • Hypotension

  • Peripheral vasodilation

  • Bradycardia (relative, due to loss of sympathetic tone)

High-yield recall:
Anaesthetics → sympathetic blockade → vasodilation → neurogenic shock.

Exam pearl:
Shock due to anaesthetics = Neurogenic shock.

Pathology 03.question: ৪০) Which of the following is not a mode of transmission of syphilis?
Pathology 03.exp:
Syphilis is primarily transmitted through contact with infectious lesions containing Treponema pallidum.

Modes include:

  • Kissing — possible when an infectious oral lesion is present.

  • Percutaneous injury — possible through contact with infected blood/tissue, especially occupational exposure.

  • Transplacental transmission — causes congenital syphilis.

Breastfeeding is not a usual mode of transmission of syphilis. However, transmission could theoretically occur if there is an active syphilitic lesion on the breast/nipple.

Exam pearl:
Classic syphilis transmission → sexual contact + transplacental; breast milk itself is not a typical route.

Pathology 03.question: ৪১) Painless regional lymphadenopathy occurs in which type of syphilis?
Pathology 03.exp:
In primary syphilis, the typical lesion is a painless, indurated chancre, accompanied by painless, firm, non-tender regional lymphadenopathy.

High-yield comparison:

  • Primary syphilis: Painless chancre + painless regional lymphadenopathy

  • Secondary syphilis: Generalized lymphadenopathy + widespread rash

  • Latent syphilis: No clinical signs

  • Tertiary syphilis: Gummas, cardiovascular and neurological manifestations

Exam pearl:
Painless chancre + painless regional nodes = Primary syphilis.

Pathology 03.question: ৪২) Causes of acute false-positive test for syphilis excludes..?
Pathology 03.exp:
Acute biological false-positive (BFP) reactions in non-treponemal syphilis tests such as VDRL/RPR can occur in several conditions, including:

  • Infectious mononucleosis

  • Chickenpox

  • Pregnancy

Poliomyelitis is not a recognized common cause of an acute false-positive syphilis test.

High-yield Syphilis recall:
Acute false-positive VDRL/RPR → viral infections + pregnancy + some other transient conditions.

Exam pearl:
Poliomyelitis = not a typical cause of acute false-positive VDRL.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৩) Obvious internal haemorrhage are called......Haemorrhage?
Pathology 03.exp:
Concealed hemorrhage is internal bleeding where the blood does not escape externally and accumulates within a body cavity or tissue.

Examples:

  • Hemothorax

  • Hemoperitoneum

  • Retroperitoneal hemorrhage

  • Intracranial hemorrhage

High-yield Hemorrhage recall:

  • Revealed hemorrhage → blood is visible externally.

  • Concealed hemorrhage → internal bleeding, not externally visible.

  • Reactionary hemorrhage → occurs within 24 hours.

  • Primary hemorrhage → occurs immediately following injury/surgery.

Exam pearl:
Obvious internal hemorrhage = Concealed hemorrhage.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৪) Which one is contraindicated in a patient of uncomplicated gonorrhoea with pregnancy?
Pathology 03.exp:
Ofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone and is generally contraindicated/avoided during pregnancy because of potential fetal toxicity.

For uncomplicated gonorrhoea in pregnancy, safer options include:

  • Ceftriaxone — preferred treatment

  • Cefixime — alternative in some guidelines

  • Spectinomycin — an alternative where available

Exam pearl:
Pregnancy + gonorrhoea → avoid fluoroquinolones such as ofloxacin; ceftriaxone is preferred.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৫) Which is not a common complications of delayed therapy in gonorrhoea?
Pathology 03.exp:
Delayed treatment of gonorrhoea can lead to ascending or local complications.

Common complications include:

  • Epididymo-orchitis → common complication in males.

  • Bartholin's gland abscess → can occur in females.

  • Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) → important complication in females and may lead to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

Proctitis can occur with gonococcal infection, particularly following rectal exposure, but it is generally considered a site of infection rather than a typical delayed complication.

Exam pearl:
Delayed gonorrhoea → Epididymo-orchitis + Bartholin abscess + PID; Proctitis is not usually listed as a common complication.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৬) All information are true about chancroid except...?
Pathology 03.exp:
Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and characteristically produces:

  • Short incubation period → usually 3–7 days

  • Painful, soft ulcers with undermined edges

  • Tender, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (often buboes)

Therefore, “painless ulcers” is the incorrect statement.

Exam pearl:
Chancroid = painful ulcer + undermined edge + tender inguinal lymph nodes.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৭) What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in anaphylactic shock?
Pathology 03.exp:
Anaphylactic shock is a severe Type-I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE.

Mechanism:
Allergen → IgE production → IgE binds mast cells/basophils → re-exposure → degranulation → histamine & other mediators → vasodilation + increased vascular permeability + bronchoconstriction → shock

High-yield Immunology recall:

  • Type I → IgE → Anaphylaxis

  • Type II → IgG/IgM → Cytotoxic

  • Type III → Immune complex

  • Type IV → T-cell mediated (delayed)

Exam pearl:
Anaphylactic shock = Type-I hypersensitivity = IgE-mediated.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৮) How many types of hemorrhage are the according to external visibility of hemorrhage?
Pathology 03.exp:
According to external visibility, hemorrhage is classified into 2 types:

  1. Revealed hemorrhage → bleeding is visible externally or escapes through a natural body opening.

  2. Concealed hemorrhage → blood remains within the body/tissues and is not externally visible.

High-yield Surgery recall:
By external visibility → Revealed + Concealed = 2 types.

Exam pearl:
External visibility অনুযায়ী hemorrhage = 2 types.

Pathology 03.question: ৪৯) Which test is done to detect bilirubin in urine?
Pathology 03.exp:
Foucher's test is used to detect bilirubin in urine. It is based on the oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin, producing a characteristic color change.

High-yield Urine test recall:

Test Detects
Foucher's test Bilirubin
Benedict's test Reducing sugars
Rothera's test Ketone bodies
Orthotolidine test Blood/hemoglobin

Exam pearl:
Urinary bilirubin → Foucher's test.

Pathology 03.question: ৫০) Which organ exhibit acute tubular necrosis due to shock?
Pathology 03.exp:
Shock causes severe hypoperfusion and ischemia of the kidneys. Prolonged renal ischemia particularly damages the renal tubular epithelium, resulting in acute tubular necrosis (ATN).

Typical sequence:

Shock → renal hypoperfusion → tubular ischemia → ATN → acute kidney injury (AKI)

Exam pearl:
Acute tubular necrosis due to shock → Kidney.
